evidence.title: The epic is centuries later than the proposed deposit
evidence.observation: The composition date is around 1200, whereas the proposed historical catastrophe belongs to the fifth century.
evidence.supports: A long interval separates the poem from the putative deposition.
evidence.doesNot: This does not establish that oral tradition preserved a real hoard.
evidence.alternative: A story can retain historical names while inventing motives, wealth and locations.
evidence.next: Commission a review of the transmission of the hoard motif, distinct from the Burgundian defeat.

evidence.title: Manuscript B is not a fifth-century witness
evidence.observation: The holding catalogue dates Cod. Sang. 857 to the third quarter of the thirteenth century, probably around 1260.
evidence.supports: The poem has a surviving medieval manuscript witness.
evidence.doesNot: A genuine manuscript does not authenticate the events it narrates.
evidence.alternative: Composition date and physical manuscript date must not be conflated.
evidence.next: Collate the hoard passage from the facsimile and a critical transcription.

evidence.title: Manuscript C provides another medieval witness
evidence.observation: The catalogue dates Cod. Donaueschingen 63 to the second quarter of the thirteenth century.
evidence.supports: A second major witness is available for comparison.
evidence.doesNot: Multiple copies of a story are not independent eyewitness accounts of a sinking.
evidence.alternative: Shared textual ancestry can explain agreement.
evidence.next: Compare wording, stanza numbering and context across A, B and C.

evidence.title: The location clue requires textual criticism
evidence.observation: The specialist survey reports the Rhine deposition at Lôche. Lettsom’s English translation renders the place as Lochheim.
evidence.supports: The literary tradition contains a location cue.
evidence.doesNot: The translation does not settle the modern location.
evidence.alternative: A translator may expand an ambiguous name using an existing interpretation.
evidence.next: Produce a verified witness-by-witness table; do not silently standardise Lôche to a modern village.

evidence.title: The hoard story changes between traditions
evidence.observation: The specialist comparison describes different owners, motives and losses in the German epic, Norse accounts and later adaptations.
evidence.supports: The treasure motif was reshaped in transmission.
evidence.doesNot: Combining every version does not create a coherent historical itinerary.
evidence.alternative: Independent literary elaboration can generate conflicting geographical clues.
evidence.next: Choose an explicitly defined tradition for each hypothesis.

evidence.title: Prosper attests a Burgundian catastrophe
evidence.observation: Prosper’s passage names Gundicharius, Aetius, an initial peace, and subsequent destruction by Huns.
evidence.supports: There is near-contemporary testimony to a ruler and catastrophe.
evidence.doesNot: The cited passage identifies no treasure, hiding place or court at Worms.
evidence.alternative: The historical event and the literary treasure can have different origins.
evidence.next: Check a critical Latin edition and chronological apparatus; the teaching page’s displayed 408 should not be repeated.

evidence.title: The Burgundian royal court at Worms is uncertain
evidence.observation: Bender’s 2023 review explicitly leaves the historical court’s location at Worms unresolved.
evidence.supports: Worms is firmly a literary setting, but weaker as an archaeological anchor.
evidence.doesNot: The poem alone cannot determine a fifth-century royal residence.
evidence.alternative: The poet may have selected an important city of his own period.
evidence.next: Review settlement archaeology and ancient geography before assigning a spatial prior to Worms.

evidence.title: A treasury is plausible but undocumented here
evidence.observation: Royal or military wealth is a plausible background to a hoard story, but no contemporary deposition record has been identified in this review.
evidence.supports: A historically possible mechanism worth specifying.
evidence.doesNot: Possibility does not show that a single treasury was hidden or survives.
evidence.alternative: Ordinary tribute, plunder and redistribution could inspire the motif without a lost cache.
evidence.next: Find independent historical or material evidence of a specific deposit; do not infer it from kingship alone.

evidence.title: Lochheim near Biebesheim is historically attested
evidence.observation: LAGIS gives an earliest attestation in 770–771 and places the deserted settlement tentatively northwest of Biebesheim.
evidence.supports: A real settlement and name existed in the medieval landscape.
evidence.doesNot: It does not establish a fifth-century settlement or the treasure location.
evidence.alternative: An authentic place-name may have been borrowed by a later storyteller.
evidence.next: Check charter originals and georeference the settlement uncertainty.

evidence.title: Flochum is a linguistic development, not a second clue
evidence.observation: The field-name reference derives Flochheim/Flochum from the older settlement name through redivision and weakening.
evidence.supports: Related names can identify a historical naming tradition.
evidence.doesNot: Several related spellings do not supply several independent pieces of evidence.
evidence.alternative: All names may descend from the same settlement label.
evidence.next: Treat related spellings as one evidence family.

evidence.title: Charter 192 is a traceable archival lead
evidence.observation: Heidelberg’s database identifies CL II 192, a surviving copy at fol. 37v, column a in the Lorscher Codex.
evidence.supports: There is a concrete record to inspect beyond modern retellings.
evidence.doesNot: Its existence alone says nothing about gold deposition.
evidence.alternative: The charter may concern ordinary property and people.
evidence.next: Read its full wording and compare other Lochheim charters.

evidence.title: The 815 donation is a source conflict
evidence.observation: LAGIS lists a donation to Hersfeld in 815; the older specialist treasure survey discusses an 815 identification in connection with Lorsch.
evidence.supports: The secondary accounts require reconciliation.
evidence.doesNot: The discrepancy cannot be resolved by choosing the more attractive narrative.
evidence.alternative: Different documents, identifications or a secondary error may be involved.
evidence.next: Inspect the actual 815 document and critical regesta before using it to locate Lôche.

evidence.title: Sandhausen has real settlement archaeology
evidence.observation: The field report describes localisation in 1993 and a gas-pipeline rescue investigation in May 2001. Surface ceramics included seventh- to fourteenth/fifteenth-century material.
evidence.supports: This alternative Lochheim has material evidence and an investigated settlement.
evidence.doesNot: It does not identify fifth-century treasure or equate this place with Lôche.
evidence.alternative: The evidence fits a long-lived medieval settlement.
evidence.next: Audit the field archive, early ceramics and sampling limits.

evidence.title: The 1131 mention is not the start of Sandhausen settlement
evidence.observation: The report distinguishes the secure 1131 church reference from earlier archaeological material and a possible 1061 reference.
evidence.supports: First written mention and earliest occupation are different questions.
evidence.doesNot: Earlier occupation still does not demonstrate a fifth-century deposit.
evidence.alternative: Document survival can make a settlement appear younger than it is.
evidence.next: Avoid dismissing the site solely because its secure written mention is late.

evidence.title: Hamm–Eich is a search hypothesis, not a verified point
evidence.observation: Jacobi associated an old river landscape around Hamm and Eich with the literary hiding place.
evidence.supports: An identifiable hypothesis can be audited.
evidence.doesNot: A modern bank position does not establish an ancient channel or deposit.
evidence.alternative: The same name tradition can be placed differently in changing river geography.
evidence.next: Recover original mapped search boundaries before any field design.

evidence.title: Rheinbach-Loch is not an excavated treasure discovery
evidence.observation: The specialist survey describes alternative name-based reconstructions and reports no excavation at the proposed Rheinbach site at the time of writing.
evidence.supports: A competing theory exists in the literature.
evidence.doesNot: This is not evidence of an unsuccessful comprehensive search, nor a current permit-status check.
evidence.alternative: Similar names may be selected after the theory is formed.
evidence.next: Require original argument, chronology and independent site evidence before field expenditure.

evidence.title: Jacobi drilling is reported, but the campaign dossier is missing
evidence.observation: Local accounts describe drilling and excavations by Hans and Hans Jörg Jacobi. Original campaign records were not available in the reviewed material.
evidence.supports: Field activity is credibly reported.
evidence.doesNot: The number, position, depth and coverage of interventions are not independently established.
evidence.alternative: Later descriptions may combine several events or repeat one source.
evidence.next: Obtain logs, plans, permits and contractor records.

evidence.title: The reported marble block is not authenticated treasure evidence
evidence.observation: Bender reports a marble block encountered at about ten metres and Jacobi’s interpretation of it as a possible covering.
evidence.supports: A physical observation has been claimed.
evidence.doesNot: No examined sample, custody record or stratigraphic report establishes a treasure association.
evidence.alternative: Building material, redeposited stone, later fill or misidentification remain possible.
evidence.next: Locate sample and borehole log; verify petrology, worked surfaces and depositional context.

evidence.title: An equipment limitation is a reported explanation
evidence.observation: Ritscher’s account says depth was underestimated and appropriate equipment for safe continuation was unavailable.
evidence.supports: An operational explanation for stopping has been reported.
evidence.doesNot: It does not prove that equipment was the only obstacle or that a deeper target exists.
evidence.alternative: The reported anomaly may have had no archaeological significance.
evidence.next: Find the contractor report, stopping depth and contemporaneous correspondence.

evidence.title: September 2003 is securely a public-claim date
evidence.observation: Gallé reports Jacobi expressing confidence at a public event. A city-hosted chronology also lists treasure searching in 2003.
evidence.supports: Public advocacy occurred by this time.
evidence.doesNot: These documents do not securely date a separate 2003 borehole or stone discovery.
evidence.alternative: A lecture about older work can become a new search event in a shortened chronology.
evidence.next: Reconcile event reporting with dated campaign documentation.

evidence.title: A 2013 interview reports dowsing as part of the search
evidence.observation: The sensor profile mentions a professional dowser alongside drilling and excavation.
evidence.supports: An identifiable account records the methods claimed by the searcher.
evidence.doesNot: A dowsing response is not a calibrated geophysical anomaly.
evidence.alternative: Expectation and selective interpretation can create apparent confirmations.
evidence.next: Separate every claimed observation by instrument, operator, date and retained data.

evidence.title: The 2007 broadcast is evidence of publicity
evidence.observation: A broadcaster press release announced the two-part Nibelungen-Code programme.
evidence.supports: The documentary can be retrieved as a source of interviews and leads.
evidence.doesNot: A filmed reconstruction or announcement is not an excavation report.
evidence.alternative: Editing can omit uncertainty and compress chronology.
evidence.next: Retrieve full episodes and credits; label reenactments and trace every technical claim to records.

evidence.title: Claims that all candidate places were surveyed are not auditable
evidence.observation: A WELT report broadly describes diving, sonar and radar searches without presenting a coverage dataset in the reviewed extract.
evidence.supports: Such searches have been reported in the press.
evidence.doesNot: The wording cannot establish that all plausible areas or depths were tested.
evidence.alternative: Surface inspection can miss buried deposits and unsearched former channels.
evidence.next: Require georeferenced tracks, instrument settings, dates and detection limits before counting negative evidence.

evidence.title: Rheingold dredging is a different kind of search
evidence.observation: SWR reports dredging for natural gold and a total recovery of roughly 300 grams.
evidence.supports: Natural gold extraction was pursued and produced a small reported yield.
evidence.doesNot: That yield does not test the existence of manufactured objects in a buried hoard.
evidence.alternative: Placer gold and deposited valuables are different target populations.
evidence.next: Keep natural-gold production outside the archaeological search-success denominator.

evidence.title: Neupotz proves recovery of a substantial ancient Rhine hoard
evidence.observation: Berlin’s museum account records over 1,000 metal objects, about 700 kilograms, recovered by dredging an Old Rhine branch between 1967 and 1997.
evidence.supports: Substantial ancient material can survive and emerge from former Rhine channels.
evidence.doesNot: This third-century assemblage is not evidence identifying a fifth-century Burgundian treasury.
evidence.alternative: Different historical loss events can create superficially similar hoards.
evidence.next: Use its recovery history and object mix to design preservation and detection scenarios.

evidence.title: Rülzheim is a real fifth-century comparison
evidence.observation: Institutional accounts describe a late antique hoard found in 2013, with a fifth-century/Hunnic-period attribution.
evidence.supports: Valuable contemporary-period assemblages occur in the broader region.
evidence.doesNot: Regional proximity and period are insufficient for a Nibelungen identification.
evidence.alternative: Elite possessions, diplomatic gifts or concealment unrelated to Burgundians may explain it.
evidence.next: Read the excavation and conservation publications before estimating how representative it is.

evidence.title: Rülzheim illustrates the cost of losing context
evidence.observation: The local institutional account describes destruction of original ground traces. A specialist study examines its elaborate folding chair.
evidence.supports: Preserving associations and stratigraphy is central to identifying a find.
evidence.doesNot: An object’s alloy or decorative style alone may not reveal its owner or reason for burial.
evidence.alternative: Several historical owners can possess objects made in the same workshop tradition.
evidence.next: Require archaeological recording before removal and independent specialist interpretation.

evidence.title: A later river map cannot directly locate a fifth-century channel
evidence.observation: Historical maps and modern topography document different moments; the regional geomorphology literature describes complex channel migration.
evidence.supports: The search must reconstruct time-specific landscapes.
evidence.doesNot: A bend shown in the eighteenth century is not proof of the same bend in 436.
evidence.alternative: Channels can migrate, be filled, be reoccupied or be removed by extraction.
evidence.next: Combine dated sediment sequences, maps and archaeological horizons.

evidence.title: The French Upper Rhine study is an analogue, not a local map
evidence.observation: Abdulkarim and colleagues combine lidar, fieldwork and sediment provenance to distinguish palaeochannel groups.
evidence.supports: A credible approach exists for reconstructing former river systems.
evidence.doesNot: Its mapped channels and conditions do not establish those at Hamm or Biebesheim.
evidence.alternative: Local geology and preservation may differ substantially.
evidence.next: Adapt the method and acquire local cores rather than transferring conclusions.

evidence.title: Existing geological data could reduce new drilling
evidence.observation: Official services provide geological records; the RLP service also describes requests for older records and inspection of cores.
evidence.supports: There is a concrete route to existing subsurface evidence.
evidence.doesNot: This review has not extracted or audited boreholes at the candidate parcels.
evidence.alternative: Records may be sparse, inaccessible or unsuitable for archaeological dating.
evidence.next: Inventory boreholes by coordinates, depth, log quality, sample survival and licence.

evidence.title: Terrain and aerial data are available but unanalysed here
evidence.observation: Official catalogues provide digital terrain models, laser data and historical aerial imagery.
evidence.supports: Existing landscape data can support the first spatial study.
evidence.doesNot: These data do not directly image buried gold and have not been interpreted for this dossier.
evidence.alternative: Modern earthworks can imitate ancient channel features.
evidence.next: Retrieve candidate-area data, check acquisition dates and compare independent layers.

evidence.title: No single geophysical technique settles the question
evidence.observation: EAC guidance emphasises target- and geology-dependent survey selection and qualified interpretation.
evidence.supports: A combined and validated investigation is appropriate.
evidence.doesNot: Buying the newest instrument does not guarantee the relevant depth or material can be detected.
evidence.alternative: Different physical contrasts produce different signals and blind spots.
evidence.next: Set measurable target classes and blind trials before procuring wide-area surveys.

evidence.title: Radar may fail in conductive sediments
evidence.observation: USGS describes strong radar attenuation from conductive materials such as clay-rich sediment and saline porewater.
evidence.supports: Local conductivity and sediments must be tested.
evidence.doesNot: A negative radar survey cannot exclude a target below its effective penetration.
evidence.alternative: A blank image may reflect signal loss, not empty ground.
evidence.next: Measure site conditions and validate depth-specific performance with representative targets.

evidence.title: Underwater surface surveys leave buried targets unresolved
evidence.observation: Underwater guidance distinguishes surface and sub-bottom methods and their interpretation.
evidence.supports: Buried deposits require methods capable of examining the subsurface.
evidence.doesNot: A clean sonar image of the riverbed cannot exclude objects below sediment.
evidence.alternative: Scour, burial, gas and substrate can change visibility.
evidence.next: Design combined bathymetric, sub-bottom and targeted verification work with a river specialist.

evidence.title: Sediment dating constrains a landscape, not the gold directly
evidence.observation: Rhine-delta research uses optical dating with radiocarbon constraints for sediment history.
evidence.supports: Appropriate dating can constrain deposition or abandonment of channels.
evidence.doesNot: A dated sediment sample does not automatically date an associated-looking metal object.
evidence.alternative: Reworked organic matter, mixed sediment and later intrusion can mislead.
evidence.next: Use stratigraphic relationships, multiple samples and explicit age uncertainty.

evidence.title: Search permissions precede fieldwork
evidence.observation: The state heritage authorities describe permission requirements for archaeological searches.
evidence.supports: A qualified project needs an agreed regulatory route.
evidence.doesNot: This dossier does not grant access, permission to dig or ownership of finds.
evidence.alternative: Even non-destructive methods can form part of regulated archaeological research.
evidence.next: Define parcels and methods with the authorities and landowners.

evidence.title: River work and protected sites add constraints
evidence.confidence: Moderate to high for general scope
evidence.observation: Official guidance addresses waterway interventions and restrictions in protected archaeological areas.
evidence.supports: Field design must account for navigation, protection and custody.
evidence.doesNot: The programme cannot assume every preferred site can be excavated.
evidence.alternative: A scientifically attractive target may be inaccessible or better preserved in place.
evidence.next: Obtain project-specific determinations and budget for conservation and access.

evidence.title: The proposal’s probabilities are assumptions
evidence.observation: The 0.006%, 0.2% and 4.3% outcomes were products of illustrative conditional assumptions, not measured historical frequencies.
evidence.supports: They show how weak links can dominate overall success.
evidence.doesNot: They are not a calibrated probability range, a confidence interval or evidence of existence.
evidence.alternative: Other defensible priors could produce much lower or higher outputs.
evidence.next: Use transparent sensitivity analysis and independent expert elicitation before funding decisions.

evidence.title: The proposal’s budget is not a costed procurement plan
evidence.observation: The €3.5–7.5 million range is a preliminary allowance for a staged programme, including contingency.
evidence.supports: It provides an initial funding scale.
evidence.doesNot: It does not establish contractor rates, permit feasibility or achievable coverage.
evidence.alternative: Deep engineering and difficult recovery could substantially change costs.
evidence.next: Obtain task-specific scopes and quotations after the archive and landscape audit.

evidence.title: No verified Nibelungen discovery was located in this review
evidence.observation: The inspected sources present hypotheses and comparative hoards, without an authenticated discovery identified as the Nibelungen treasure.
evidence.supports: No reviewed positive find resolves the question.
evidence.doesNot: This is not proof of absence or an exhaustive audit of unpublished archives.
evidence.alternative: Relevant records may be offline, private, uncatalogued or lost.
evidence.next: Complete the acquisition queue and publish search limits explicitly.

evidence.title: Repeated Jacobi stories are not independent confirmations
evidence.observation: The reviewed reports repeatedly concern the same searcher and proposed location, without independent raw datasets.
evidence.supports: They document a persistent claim family.
evidence.doesNot: Several articles cannot be counted as several successful detections.
evidence.alternative: One original claim can generate a large chain of apparently corroborating reports.
evidence.next: Build a source genealogy linking every statement to its earliest record.

evidence.title: Negative evidence needs a defined detection probability
evidence.observation: A negative result is informative only in proportion to the chance that the investigation would detect a present target.
evidence.supports: A documented survey can lower belief in a narrowly specified hypothesis.
evidence.doesNot: Repeated weak searches cannot prove global non-existence.
evidence.alternative: Shared blind spots make repeated tests correlated.
evidence.next: Specify target geometry, depth, surveyed volume and a validated end-to-end probability.

evidence.title: Rülzheim has laboratory evidence, but no named owner
evidence.confidence: High for the reported analyses; limited for historical attribution
evidence.observation: CEZA reports a radiocarbon date on an olive stone associated with chair filling and analyses of silver and solder.
evidence.supports: Independent material analysis contributes to object chronology and possible manufacture or repair connections.
evidence.doesNot: It does not directly date the whole deposit or link it to the Nibelungen story.
evidence.alternative: An object can have a production, repair and deposition history spanning different dates and places.
evidence.next: Read the complete chair study and laboratory data alongside the conservation record.

evidence.title: The Lochheim report records a medieval sediment transition
evidence.confidence: High for the published observation; interpretation requires local context
evidence.observation: The rescue report describes redeposited loess above organic mud and interprets a medieval change in the local water system.
evidence.supports: Local stratigraphy can constrain landscape history more directly than place-name resemblance.
evidence.doesNot: This is not a fifth-century Rhine reconstruction or a treasure-bearing layer.
evidence.alternative: Sediment processes vary spatially; this section cannot be transferred to Hamm.
evidence.next: Review original profiles, sample locations and the dating basis.

evidence.title: Two dated maps illustrate historical river landscapes
evidence.confidence: High for catalogue dates; untested for spatial precision
evidence.observation: An archive map of the Worms area and an engineering map at Ketsch are available as credited reproductions.
evidence.supports: They are inspectable historical map sources for their stated periods.
evidence.doesNot: Neither is a fifth-century reconstruction, a survey boundary, or Jacobi’s cited 1760 map.
evidence.alternative: A historical plan may show intended works as well as contemporary features; consult its legend.
evidence.next: Retrieve complete catalogue information and georeference suitable originals with control-point errors.

evidence.title: Matched map extracts allow a reproducible landscape comparison
evidence.confidence: High for source identification; local spatial accuracy unquantified
evidence.observation: HIL historical maps and the BKG basemap are rendered on the same Web Mercator grid and identical pixel bounds for each area.
evidence.supports: Broad changes in settlement extent, water bodies and channel configuration can be inspected by swipe or transparency.
evidence.doesNot: Identical output coordinates do not eliminate historical survey error, cartographic displacement or differences in map generalisation.
evidence.alternative: Map compilation, changing symbols and uneven revision can resemble physical change. Inspect the source dates and the shared geography.
evidence.next: Check original sheets and independent stable control points; test inferred changes against dated air photos, engineering records and cores.

evidence.title: The Kühkopf cutoff changed flow and sedimentation
evidence.confidence: High for source identification; local spatial accuracy unquantified
evidence.observation: The Hessian education centre dates the opening to 30 April 1829 and describes increased sedimentation in the old arm after the cutoff.
evidence.supports: Today’s land and narrow watercourses can occupy a former active river bed.
evidence.doesNot: This does not establish the Rhine’s fifth-century position or the preservation of a particular deposit.
evidence.alternative: Map compilation, changing symbols and uneven revision can resemble physical change. Inspect the source dates and the shared geography.
evidence.next: Check original sheets and independent stable control points; test inferred changes against dated air photos, engineering records and cores.

evidence.title: Later maps show additional water bodies and expanded settlements
evidence.observation: Visual comparison of the early and modern extracts shows extensive lake areas near Eich and larger built-up areas around Biebesheim and Hamm.
evidence.supports: Modern surface conditions and disturbance must enter a search model.
evidence.doesNot: Map comparison alone cannot give excavation depth, sediment survival, exact construction dates or the age of an underlying palaeochannel.
evidence.alternative: Map compilation, changing symbols and uneven revision can resemble physical change. Inspect the source dates and the shared geography.
evidence.next: Check original sheets and independent stable control points; test inferred changes against dated air photos, engineering records and cores.

evidence.title: Specific pre-cutoff archive maps are available
evidence.confidence: High for source identification; local spatial accuracy unquantified
evidence.observation: The archive catalogues Born’s map at 1723, with original dating 1723–1725, and Hoehle’s Kühkopf map at 1822.
evidence.supports: These are concrete sources to extend the landscape chronology earlier than the aligned survey mosaic.
evidence.doesNot: Neither has been georeferenced here; neither is the unverified 1760 map cited in Jacobi-related accounts.
evidence.alternative: Map compilation, changing symbols and uneven revision can resemble physical change. Inspect the source dates and the shared geography.
evidence.next: Check original sheets and independent stable control points; test inferred changes against dated air photos, engineering records and cores.

legend.title: A story is the starting point
legend.question: What would turn a famous legend into an archaeological case?
legend.text: The treasure enters our investigation through a medieval epic. A historical catastrophe, a real place-name and a lost deposit are three separate claims to test.
legend.clue: The literary tradition gives us a Rhine deposition and the name Lôche.
legend.open: No authenticated Nibelungen hoard was identified in the sources reviewed.
legend.next: Separate what the poem says from what contemporary evidence can establish.

sections.title: What are we actually looking for?
sections.text: The first task is to define “the treasure”. A literal reading asks whether the particular hoard in the Nibelungenlied was deposited as described. A broader archaeological question asks whether a recoverable late antique hoard survives somewhere in the region. A third question asks whether any discovery could be connected to the people behind the legend. Finding ancient metal would answer only part of this sequence.

sections.title: Read the poem as a source
sections.text: In the epic, the hoard is wealth that gives its holder power. Hagen removes it from Kriemhild’s control and the poem places its sinking in the Rhine at Lôche. Later versions change the person who loses the treasure and the circumstances. These differences matter: combining details from different stories can produce an attractive search narrative that no single source actually contains.

sections.title: Our working decision
sections.text: We should keep the literal-legend and historical-hoard hypotheses separate throughout the programme. Before fieldwork, write down what material, date range, deposit setting and minimum recoverable size would count as a target. A result outside that definition can still be an important discovery; it simply answers a different question. This is a proposed research rule, not an assertion that such a deposit exists.

gap.title: Seven centuries to bridge
gap.question: How far is the poem from the events behind it?
gap.text: The epic was composed around 1200. Its proposed historical setting is the fifth century. The surviving manuscripts are later still.
gap.clue: The medieval manuscripts are real, traceable objects.
gap.open: Their authenticity does not make the treasure story an eyewitness account.
gap.next: Compare the hoard passage across the principal manuscript witnesses.

sections.title: Three dates, three different things
sections.text: The composition of the Nibelungenlied around 1200, the copying of a surviving manuscript, and a proposed fifth-century historical background are distinct dates. Manuscript C at Karlsruhe is catalogued to the second quarter of the thirteenth century. Manuscript B at St Gallen is generally placed later in that century. The page reproduced here is the opening of C, not the treasure passage.

sections.title: The word that becomes a destination
sections.text: A modern translation can silently turn an ambiguous place-name into a specific place on today’s map. The English reading edition used in this dossier gives Lochheim, but that translation is not independent evidence for the location. The necessary next step is a side-by-side comparison of the original wording in A, B and C, using folio images, a critical edition and a specialist’s account of the name. That collation has not yet been done.

sections.title: What an archive result could change
sections.text: If the principal witnesses support a narrower geographical reading, the candidate list could shrink. If the name remains ambiguous or has a literary explanation, searching one modern village becomes harder to justify. Neither outcome would prove that no unrelated ancient hoard exists. The useful product is an annotated passage with every interpretive step exposed.

court.title: Was the royal court at Worms?
court.question: How secure is the anchor on our map?
court.text: Prosper records a Burgundian ruler and catastrophe. The cited passage supplies no treasure location. A specialist historical review leaves the royal court at Worms unresolved.
court.clue: Near-contemporary testimony supports part of the historical framework.
court.open: A literary setting cannot, by itself, locate an ancient treasury.
court.next: Review ancient geography and settlement archaeology independently of the poem.

sections.title: The historical anchor is incomplete
sections.text: Prosper’s chronicle supplies near-contemporary testimony concerning a Burgundian ruler and a destructive defeat. It does not describe a hidden treasury or give a findspot. The university teaching page used here also has a problematic displayed year, so the chronology needs checking against a critical edition before it becomes a fixed point in a project timeline.

sections.title: Why Worms belongs on the map
sections.text: Worms is central to the literary setting and to the modern commemoration of the story. The specialist review in this dossier nevertheless treats the location of a fifth-century Burgundian royal court as uncertain. A monument, a festival, and a medieval narrative can all document the reception of a legend without independently establishing the ancient administrative centre.

sections.title: A test worth funding
sections.text: Build a dated inventory of settlement traces, cemeteries, inscriptions and stray finds across the wider region. Evaluate how securely each can be dated and whether any ethnic attribution is justified. This work could test assumptions about settlement and political geography. A distribution map should show gaps in investigation as well as finds, because an empty area can reflect missing observation rather than absent occupation.

lochheim.title: A real name, an unresolved place
lochheim.question: Is this Lochheim the poem’s Lôche?
lochheim.text: Official records attest a medieval Lochheim near Biebesheim. That is a useful geographical lead. The step from this settlement to a fifth-century treasure remains unproven.
lochheim.clue: Dated charters and a historical place-name register can be checked.
lochheim.open: Related spellings are one naming tradition, not independent treasure clues.
lochheim.next: Resolve the charter geography and the conflicting accounts of the 815 donation.

sections.title: Why this lead deserves attention
sections.text: The historical gazetteer documents a deserted Lochheim near Biebesheim, with early medieval name forms and a location that is not completely secure. The survival of related field names offers a route into cadastral and charter research. It does not take the settlement back automatically to the fifth century or identify it with the poem’s Lôche.

sections.title: One tradition can look like several clues
sections.text: Lochheim, Flochheim and Flochum are related names, not three separate discoveries of a treasure location. Accounts also disagree about the 815 donation. The dossier keeps this discrepancy open rather than selecting whichever version best suits a search theory. A charter must be checked for its date, copying history, people, neighbouring properties and the place it actually identifies.

sections.title: Make the geography reproducible
sections.text: The proposed output is a map with separate layers for charter references, later property boundaries, historical river channels and modern parcels. Each point should carry an uncertainty area rather than false precision. The eighteenth-century Worms map in this gallery is an example of a dated cartographic source; it is not the specific 1760 map invoked in Jacobi-related accounts.

sandhausen.title: Another Lochheim has archaeology
sandhausen.question: Does a late first mention mean a late settlement?
sandhausen.text: A rescue excavation near Sandhausen provides material evidence for a medieval settlement. Earlier ceramics make its secure 1131 written mention an inadequate starting date.
sandhausen.clue: There is an original, published field report to investigate.
sandhausen.open: Settlement evidence does not identify the poem’s hiding place or a fifth-century hoard.
sandhausen.next: Inspect the excavation archive, finds chronology and sampling limits.

sections.title: What the field report actually records
sections.text: Hildebrandt and Gross describe a gas-pipeline rescue investigation in May 2001 at the northern edge of the deserted settlement. Surface collections ranged from the seventh to the fourteenth or fifteenth centuries. A roughly 1.8-metre-wide sunken building contained burning traces and early medieval ceramics; its filling was placed before or around the year 1000. This is substantially more informative than a first written mention alone.

sections.title: The sediment tells another story
sections.text: Across about 250 metres, the report describes yellow redeposited loess over dark organic mud and older loess below. The authors connected the change in sedimentation with medieval alteration of the local water system. Our section drawing simplifies those reported layers; it is not a measured excavation profile and does not show a treasure.

sections.title: What remains to be tested
sections.text: This evidence weakens the argument that a secure mention in 1131 must mean a settlement began that late. It does not establish fifth-century occupation, nor does a narrow pipeline investigation test the whole landscape. Request the plans, finds catalogue and original documentation before drawing a boundary around either the settlement or a future search.

jacobi.title: The ten-metre claim
jacobi.question: What did the drill actually encounter?
jacobi.text: Accounts describe Jacobi’s drilling and a marble block at about ten metres. The original log, sample and archaeological context have not been inspected.
jacobi.clue: A claimed physical observation could, in principle, be re-examined.
jacobi.open: Stone, depth and interpretation are all dependent on records still missing.
jacobi.next: Locate the campaign archive and any surviving sample before drilling again.

sections.title: The reported intervention
sections.text: Published accounts associate Hans and Hans Jörg Jacobi with work in the Hamm–Eich area from the 1970s onward. A specialist synthesis describes a marble block recovered at about ten metres on the Hofgut Seibert property. The original borehole location, drilling log, sample accession and photographs were not available for this dossier. The illustration is therefore a diagram of the claim, not a reconstruction of a documented borehole.

sections.title: Why work reportedly stopped
sections.text: Ritscher’s local account attributes the interruption to underestimated depth and unsuitable equipment for continuing safely. This is a reported operational explanation, not an independently established failure analysis. We cannot infer that better machinery would have reached treasure. A stone could be natural, displaced, reused or otherwise unrelated; its interpretation depends on material identification and context.

sections.title: Untangle the dates before counting searches
sections.text: Gallé describes a public statement of confidence in September 2003. That establishes an announcement, not necessarily a new drilling campaign that year. Later interviews and broadcasts can repeat the same older observation. The archive audit should connect every reported event to a dated primary record, and record explicitly when several articles derive from a single claim.

negative.title: An empty search has conditions
negative.question: Would that search have found a present target?
negative.text: A search result is only as strong as its documented coverage and detection ability. Broad press accounts do not tell us which places, depths and target sizes were actually tested.
negative.clue: Logs, tracks and calibration can turn a negative result into useful evidence.
negative.open: Repeated searches can share the same blind spots.
negative.next: Define the target and survey volume, then validate detection in local sediments.

sections.title: “Nothing found” is not one kind of result
sections.text: A negative survey can mean the instrument worked in a fully observed area and found no target, or that coverage, depth or sensitivity were inadequate. Without tracks, settings, sediment conditions and quality-control records, those cases cannot be separated. The reviewed media summaries do not provide enough information to treat the whole Rhine or a complete candidate area as excluded.

sections.title: Specify what the search could have seen
sections.text: A compact chest of metal, scattered coins and a stone-lined feature are different targets. A technique that detects one may miss another at the same depth. Future work should record the smallest target it reliably detects, the tested burial range and the amount of inaccessible or disturbed ground. The illustrated grid shows why repeating the same survey can repeat the same blind spots.

sections.title: A numerical example, not a forecast
sections.text: Suppose a location begins with a 10% assumed chance of containing the defined target. Suppose the search covers half of the possible positions and detects 80% of targets in that covered part. Its overall detection chance is 40%; after a negative result the conditional presence probability is 6.25%. These are deliberately chosen teaching inputs. The probability explorer lets you change them; real values require evidence.

neupotz.title: A real hoard from the Rhine
neupotz.question: What can a different treasure teach us?
neupotz.text: The Neupotz assemblage demonstrates that substantial ancient metalwork can survive in former Rhine channels. Its chronology and identity are distinct from the Nibelungen claim.
neupotz.clue: The museum documents a large assemblage recovered over decades.
neupotz.open: One successful recovery does not tell us the frequency of undiscovered hoards.
neupotz.next: Use the recovery history to study preservation and detection, not to establish identity.

sections.title: Look beyond the word “treasure”
sections.text: Neupotz is a substantial Roman-period metal assemblage recovered during gravel extraction from an old Rhine channel. Museum presentations include vessels, tools, vehicle components, locks and shackles. The photographed shackles are actual objects from that separate assemblage. A large hoard need not look like a box of gold coins; its composition affects how it survives and how a survey might detect it.

sections.title: What this comparison can and cannot do
sections.text: The museum dates the loss to the third century. That separates it from the fifth-century setting proposed for the Burgundian story. Its recovery demonstrates survival in a river landscape, but it supplies neither a rate of undiscovered hoards nor the probability of finding another. The recovery process also matters: objects lifted by industrial extraction do not retain the same contextual information as a controlled excavation.

sections.title: A useful technical comparison
sections.text: Commission a recovery-history review: where objects were brought up, which sediment was removed, how dispersed the assemblage was and what documentation survives. Use that review to define preservation and detection questions. Do not transfer a successful discovery’s dimensions, date or identity onto an unrelated signal in another part of the floodplain.

ruelzheim.title: The right period is not an identity
ruelzheim.question: Would fifth-century valuables settle the legend?
ruelzheim.text: Rülzheim offers a real late antique comparison. Matching period and broad region would still be insufficient to name a new discovery as the legendary treasure.
ruelzheim.clue: A valuable fifth-century assemblage exists in the wider region.
ruelzheim.open: Lost excavation context limits what can be said about ownership and concealment.
ruelzheim.next: Preserve every association and stratigraphic relationship in any future investigation.

sections.title: An object can preserve laboratory clues
sections.text: The late antique Rülzheim hoard includes a remarkable silver folding chair. CEZA’s 2018 report describes an olive stone found in filling material associated with a small bust. Radiocarbon analysis placed that organic material in the late fourth or early fifth century. This dates a sample associated with an object component; it is not a direct date for the concealment of the whole hoard.

sections.title: Composition can test a production history
sections.text: The laboratory also investigated the chair’s metal and solder. The solder’s lead-isotope composition was compatible with Eifel deposits and with solder on a broadly contemporary Trier silver jug. CEZA considered manufacture or repair near Trier possible. Such matches can narrow a technological discussion, but they do not name an owner or establish a connection to Gunther, Hagen or the Nibelungen story.

sections.title: Context is part of the discovery
sections.text: The circumstances of recovery limit reconstruction of the original deposit. The research lesson is to preserve associations, positions and conservation evidence from the beginning. Our illustration separates an organic date, a metal-provenance argument and a deposit history. They answer different questions, and should never be compressed into “the treasure has been identified”.

landscape.title: The river has moved
landscape.question: Are we looking in the channel that existed then?
landscape.text: A modern river bend or an eighteenth-century map cannot fix the fifth-century river. Dated sediment, historical maps and existing boreholes have to be studied together.
landscape.clue: Geological archives and terrain data provide a practical starting point.
landscape.open: No candidate-area palaeochannel model has been completed for this dossier.
landscape.next: Map surviving deposits and extraction history before choosing survey parcels.

sections.title: A real historical map, at its own date
sections.text: The gallery now includes a 1736 map of the Worms–Lampertheim area from the Hessian State Archive and an 1833 map illustrating the Ketsch Rhine cutoff. They make changing river geography tangible. Neither image establishes a fifth-century channel, and neither has been georeferenced here. Look at the original legend and orientation before comparing it with the modern atlas.

sections.title: A published example of the method
sections.text: Abdulkarim and colleagues mapped former channels in the French Upper Rhine plain using terrain data, aerial images and old maps, then investigated selected channels with cores. The reproduced figures show their terrain and reconstructed network in Alsace. They are a methodological comparison south of our principal candidates, not survey results for Hamm or Biebesheim.

sections.title: What to build for this project
sections.text: Start with existing boreholes, historical cartography, elevation models and extraction records. Distinguish deposits that survive, deposits that have been removed, and areas whose history is unknown. Then obtain age constraints on selected sediment sequences. The result should be a time-specific three-dimensional search volume with uncertainties, not a single attractive bend circled on a map.

methods.title: Prove the method can see the target
methods.question: Which tool can answer the question at this depth?
methods.text: Radar, electromagnetic methods and underwater surveys respond to different physical contrasts. Local sediment and target form determine whether a negative result has meaning.
methods.clue: Blind trials can measure performance against representative targets.
methods.open: No candidate-site trial has established the detection probabilities used in the proposal.
methods.next: Require independent calibration before commissioning wide-area work.

sections.title: Match the instrument to the physical question
sections.text: Radar measures contrasts in electromagnetic properties; its useful depth is constrained by the ground. Magnetometry responds to magnetic contrasts and is not a direct gold detector. Electrical and electromagnetic surveys can help characterize sediment or conductive targets, but an anomaly still needs interpretation. No method in this dossier has yet passed a local target-detection trial.

sections.title: Treat the river bed and buried sediments separately
sections.text: Bathymetry maps the bed surface; side-scan sonar can reveal exposed objects and texture. Sub-bottom methods investigate sediment structure under suitable conditions. A clean surface image does not exclude an object below sediment. These are different observation volumes, so a survey report must state what was visible and what remained beyond its effective depth or resolution.

sections.title: A field decision we can audit
sections.text: Use independent blind trials with representative targets and local sediments before scaling up. Agree how a candidate will be revisited by a second method, what counts as a significant anomaly and which observations would stop further spending. Record detection misses as carefully as successes. These proposed quality controls are the bridge from illustrative probability sliders to evidence-based survey planning.

decision.title: Search for a testable answer
decision.question: Which missing record would change your view most?
decision.text: The immediate priority is an archive and landscape audit. A sample with provenance, an original log, or a corrected place identification could sharply redirect the programme.
decision.clue: The dossier gives each claim a source trail and a next decisive check.
decision.open: Numerical success scenarios remain assumptions, not calibrated forecasts.
decision.next: Evaluate the evidence, rank the missing records, and agree a stopping rule.

sections.title: Success has more than one level
sections.text: A programme can succeed by rejecting a specific location, establishing that an old search claim cannot be substantiated, locating a real archaeological deposit, or recovering evidence that changes the historical interpretation. The much stronger claim that a find is the legendary Nibelungen hoard needs independent support. Define these outcomes before investing, so an interesting object is not mistaken for the answer to every question.

sections.title: A sequence for an ambitious programme
sections.text: First recover and assess the campaign archive and the key texts. Next reconstruct candidate landscapes and prioritize surviving deposits. Then validate instruments locally and survey only justified areas. Finally, investigate a reproducible anomaly through an agreed archaeological project with conservation and publication built in. Each stage should finish with an explicit continue, revise or stop decision.

sections.title: What we can honestly rule out
sections.text: A negative result can exclude a specified target in a specified volume to a measured detection standard. It cannot prove that no treasure ever existed anywhere, especially if a deposit was recovered, dispersed or destroyed long ago. The immediate goal is therefore to turn a broad legend into a set of bounded claims that can actually be tested. The probability figures remain scenario assumptions until that work supplies better inputs.

videos.title: Der Schatz der Nibelungen
videos.summary: The broadcaster describes a search involving old texts, the disappeared Lochheim and modern treasure hunters. This is the closest match to the central question in this atlas.
videos.watch: Look for the original document behind each location claim, and whether any detector result is independently verified.
videos.limit: A documentary’s proposed connections are leads to audit. Its description does not establish a discovered hoard, and a broadcast is not a drilling log.

videos.title: Das Nibelungenlied
videos.publisher: ZDF · Terra X / ZDF goes Schule
videos.summary: An interpretation centred on Kriemhild and the medieval society reflected in the poem. Useful alongside the manuscript chronology and the distinction between literary setting and ancient testimony.
videos.watch: Separate the world of the poem’s composition from the much earlier events it may rework.
videos.limit: This supplies a literary perspective, not an ancient location fix. The provider lists availability until 12 December 2031.

videos.title: Die Nibelungensage in 90 Sekunden
videos.publisher: Terra X History · official YouTube channel
videos.summary: A very short introduction to the story’s characters and treasure. Best used as an orientation before the evidence chapters.
videos.watch: Notice how compression makes several strands of the tradition look like one continuous account.
videos.limit: A popular retelling should not substitute for comparing manuscript witnesses or be used to estimate treasure value.

videos.title: Der Rhein (1/2)
videos.english: The Rhine as a changing historical landscape
videos.summary: A broad account of settlement, trade and major events along the Rhine, including the Nibelungen tradition. It places river finds in a much longer history of activity along the waterway.
videos.watch: Ask which scenes concern the Upper Rhine study area and which concern other reaches of the river.
videos.limit: Regional history does not date a channel at Hamm. Use the aligned maps and local sediment studies for that question.

videos.title: Historische Karten mit QGIS georeferenzieren
videos.english: How historical map overlays are made
videos.summary: A technical demonstration of aligning historical maps with modern coordinates, using control points and printed grids. The speakers explain how map scale, displacement and historical coordinate systems complicate the work.
videos.watch: The sections on control-point selection and coordinate systems explain why an attractive overlay can still mislead.
videos.limit: This teaches a method. It neither surveys the treasure candidates nor independently validates the alignment error of our map extracts.

videos.title: Das Nibelungenlied · Sommers Weltliteratur
videos.date: Publication date not stated on the reviewed page
videos.summary: A compact German-language explanation of the epic’s plot, useful for keeping the characters and sequence of events straight while evaluating the treasure story.
videos.watch: Use it to orient yourself, then return to the manuscript and historical-source records.
videos.limit: An educational plot summary is not archaeological evidence. Open the provider page to load its YouTube player.

mapComparison.method: Tiles supplied in EPSG:3857; assembled and cropped to identical global pixel bounds. No manual warp. Approximate geographic boxes describe study windows; pixels and world-file coefficients specify actual image bounds. HIL historical georeferencing residuals not independently measured.
